analysis.one_liner: Set new vehicle safety standards for brakes, pedals, and electronics and let the public see automakers' defect reports.
analysis.headline: The House Energy and Commerce Committee approved the bill 31-21 on July 14, 2010, but the full House never voted on it before Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: Written in the wake of the Toyota sudden-acceleration recalls, the bill would have required automakers to build brake-override systems, redundant accelerator controls, and clearer pedals and gear selectors into new cars. It would have put event data recorders ('black boxes') in all new cars starting model year 2015, with the data owned by the vehicle owner and access restricted. It would also have opened up automakers' internal defect reports to public view, raised maximum fines for safety violations from $15 million to $200 million, charged automakers a $3-$9 per-vehicle fee to fund the safety agency, and barred senior safety regulators from lobbying their old agency for a year.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers, passengers, and pedestrians — including blind pedestrians, who would get a minimum sound requirement for quiet electric and hybrid vehicles. Buyers would get public access to the defect data automakers report to regulators, a defect-complaint notice in the glove compartment, and searchable recall information online. The safety agency itself would get a dedicated funding stream and stronger enforcement powers.

how_it_helps.text: Required rules to mitigate unintended acceleration through brake-override systems and at least one redundant mechanism in accelerator control systems, so a driver can stop the car even when the accelerator is stuck or the electronics fail.
Required rulemakings on pedal clearance, electronic system performance standards, push-button ignition operation in emergencies, and clearer gear-selector positions.

Would have required every new passenger car sold in model year 2015 onward to carry an event data recorder, with the data owned by the owner or lessee and retrievable only with the owner's consent, a court order, or by a safety agency with personal information stripped out.
Required public disclosure of the 'early warning' defect and injury data automakers report to the safety agency, with a presumption in favor of maximum public availability.
Raised civil penalties from $5,000 to $25,000 per violation, and the cap for a related series of violations from $15 million to $200 million, and created expedited 'imminent hazard' orders.
Barred senior NHTSA safety officials from appearing before the agency on behalf of a manufacturer for one year after leaving, with fines up to $55,000.
Required a minimum alert sound on electric and hybrid vehicles so blind and other pedestrians can detect them, and funded research on technology to prevent drunk driving.

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, who would bear the cost of new safety hardware, a per-vehicle certification fee ($3, rising to $9 and adjusted with inflation), and dramatically higher penalty exposure — costs likely to be partly passed on in car prices. The bill also preserved state lawsuits over vehicle defects, a litigation exposure manufacturers wanted closed.
analysis.who_pays_short: Car makers through fees and rules

drawbacks.text: The per-vehicle safety fee ($3 the first year, $6 the second, $9 the third, indexed thereafter) and compliance costs for new hardware would raise vehicle prices for buyers, and the bill acknowledges the need to avoid 'undue adverse economic impacts on small businesses.'

Mandating continuous event data recorders in every new car raises surveillance and privacy concerns, though the bill addresses them by making the data the owner's property and restricting who can retrieve it.

Two of the most-wanted standards — pedal clearance and minimum performance standards for vehicle electronics — were written as 'consider' mandates: the agency would only impose them if it found them 'reasonable, practicable, and appropriate,' so the bill's strongest-sounding provisions were partly discretionary.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For buyers, the safety gains — brakes that beat a stuck accelerator, backup controls against electronic failure, public visibility into defect records, and real penalties for hiding safety problems — plausibly outweigh the modest per-vehicle cost; a $9 fee is a rounding error on a $30,000 car. The privacy design of the black-box mandate was unusually careful for its time. The genuine weaknesses are the discretionary standards and the fact that most of the burden of proof still fell on the regulator rather than the manufacturer.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared committee with a 31-21 vote and was placed on the House calendar in July 2010, but no floor vote was ever scheduled, and it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Waxman introduced the Motor Vehicle Safety Act of 2010 on May 25, 2010, with four Democratic cosponsors, after the Toyota unintended-acceleration recalls.
The Energy and Commerce Committee considered and marked up the bill the very next day, May 26, and ordered it reported 31-21.
The committee reported an amended bill on July 14, 2010 (H. Rept. 111-536), and it was placed on the Union Calendar, meaning it was waiting for a floor vote.
No further action was ever taken; the House never voted on the bill, and it expired at the end of the 111th Congress on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers came out ahead: they avoided the per-vehicle safety fee, a thirteenfold increase in maximum fines, mandatory public disclosure of their internal defect reports, new braking and electronics mandates, and the one-year lobbying ban for former safety regulators.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Automakers, who avoided fees and new rules

for.name: Henry A. Waxman
for.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it through his committee, which reported it amended on July 14, 2010.

for.name: 4 of 253 House Democrats
for.role: Original cosponsors (Reps. Rush, Dingell, Stupak, and Braley)

for.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee majority
for.what_they_did: Voted 31-21 to order the bill reported amended the day after introduction.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote after it was placed on the calendar in July 2010; the bill died there when the Congress ended.

against.name: 21 members of the House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Voted against ordering the bill reported at the May 26, 2010 markup.

against.name: Automobile manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed the bill's public disclosure of internal defect data, its higher penalties, and its per-vehicle fee during the 2010 debate.

sides.party_line_note: The committee's 31-21 vote to advance the bill, one day after it was introduced, was a margin consistent with most majority-party Democrats supporting it and most Republicans opposing it; the full House never voted, so there is no chamber-wide roll call to measure the split.

industries.note: The bill imposed new safety hardware, a per-vehicle certification fee, a thirteenfold increase in maximum fines, public disclosure of internal defect and injury reports, and a certification requirement making a named safety official accountable for what the company tells regulators. Its interest in killing the bill ran against buyers' interest in knowing about defects and safer cars.

Mandates for brake-override systems, redundant throttle controls, stability technology on large trucks, and alert sounds on electric vehicles would create markets for the companies that make that equipment.
